passage: The Delhi Sultanate was a complex period of history with many unique administrative systems. One key feature was the Iqta system, where the Sultan assigned tracts of land called Iqtas to military commanders known as Muqtis. These Muqtis were responsible for maintaining troops and collecting revenue, but they did not own the land; their positions were transferable and not hereditary. Another important group were the Bandagan, who were special slaves purchased for military service. Unlike common laborers, these individuals were trained to hold high political offices and positions of trust, often becoming more reliable than the Sultan's own nobles. Regarding the economy, Alauddin Khalji implemented strict market controls. He fixed the prices of all goods, from food grains to horses, primarily to maintain a large standing army at a low cost, rather than for social welfare. Finally, the authors of Tawarikh were learned men like secretaries and courtiers who lived in cities. They wrote histories to gain rich rewards from Sultans and rarely focused on the lives of ordinary peasants or villagers, whose struggles remained largely unrecorded in these official accounts.

items.evidence: These Muqtis were responsible for maintaining troops and collecting revenue, but they did not own the land; their positions were transferable and not hereditary.
items.q: A Muqti's son hopes to take over his father's Iqta. Can he claim it?
options: He cannot, because the post was not passed down
He can, because Iqta posts always passed to sons
He can, because his father owned the Iqta land
He cannot, because Iqta was only a religious tax
items.explain: Muqtis did not own the land, and their posts were transferable, not passed from father to son.

wrong.why: thinks the Muqti's post was hereditary
thinks Muqtis owned the Iqta land
thinks Iqta was a religious tax, not land

items.evidence: Unlike common laborers, these individuals were trained to hold high political offices and positions of trust, often becoming more reliable than the Sultan's own nobles.
items.q: Why might a Sultan depend on his Bandagan more than on his nobles?
options: They were trained for top posts and stayed loyal
They did his household chores without complaining
They were born into the Sultan's noble families
They paid him the Iqta tax on time
items.explain: Bandagan were trained for high offices and positions of trust, often proving more reliable than nobles.

wrong.why: mixes up purchased slaves with nobles by birth
thinks Iqta was a tax people paid

items.evidence: He fixed the prices of all goods, from food grains to horses, primarily to maintain a large standing army at a low cost, rather than for social welfare.
items.q: Why did Alauddin Khalji fix the prices of goods in the markets?
options: To keep a big army without spending much
To help the poor buy cheap food grains
To stop horse traders becoming too powerful
To raise money for shifting his capital
items.explain: Alauddin fixed prices mainly to keep a large army at low cost, not for social welfare.

wrong.why: thinks price control was to help the poor
grabs the nearby detail about horses
mixes Alauddin up with Tughluq's capital shift

items.q: A student wants to learn how peasants lived under the Sultans. How useful are the Tawarikh?
options: Not very, as writers mostly wrote for Sultans' rewards
Very, as they describe village life in detail
Very, as their authors lived among the villagers
Not very, as Sultans wrote them all themselves
